lessons.title: Turning records into performance indicators
lessons.html:
From data to information

Raw records only become useful when they are processed into information that answers a management question. At N5 level the focus moves from capturing data to analysing it: calculating performance indicators, summarising large sets of records and presenting results so that managers can act.

Common farm performance indicators

IndicatorCalculation
Calving percentageCalves born / cows mated x 100
Weaning percentageCalves weaned / cows mated x 100
Mortality rateDeaths / average number of animals x 100
Feed conversion ratio (FCR)kg feed eaten / kg live mass gained
Crop yieldTotal tonnes harvested / hectares harvested
Milk per cow per dayTotal litres / (cows in milk x days)
Cost per unitTotal cost of enterprise / units produced (e.g. R per tonne, R per litre)

Worked example

A herd of 240 cows is mated. 204 calves are born and 192 are weaned.

  • Calving percentage = 204 / 240 x 100 = 85%
  • Weaning percentage = 192 / 240 x 100 = 80%

The 5 percentage-point gap between calving and weaning points to calf losses between birth and weaning, which the manager would investigate using the death and treatment records.

Summary statistics

  • Mean – the average: sum of values divided by the number of values.
  • Median – the middle value when values are sorted; less affected by extreme values.
  • Range – highest minus lowest value; a quick indication of variation.

Example: weaning weights of five calves are 180, 195, 200, 205 and 260 kg. The mean is 208 kg, but the median is 200 kg; the one heavy calf pulls the mean up. Reporting both gives a truer picture.

Data quality before analysis

Before calculating, clean the data: remove duplicates, check for impossible values, fill or flag missing values and make sure units are consistent. Analysis of bad data produces confident but wrong conclusions.

lessons.title: Comparing, presenting and interpreting results
lessons.html:
Making comparisons

An indicator on its own means little. Its value comes from comparison:

  • Over time – this season against previous seasons, to show trends.
  • Between units – block against block, camp against camp, sire group against sire group.
  • Against targets – actual versus budgeted or planned figures.
  • Against benchmarks – results of similar farms from study groups, industry organisations or advisors.

When comparing, make sure like is compared with like: the same units, the same period and similar conditions. A dryland maize yield should not be benchmarked against irrigated yields.

Presenting data

PurposeSuitable format
Exact values for referenceTable
Trend over time (monthly rainfall, milk yield)Line graph
Comparing categories (yield per block)Bar chart
Relationship between two variables (fertiliser rate vs yield)Scatter plot

Good presentation uses clear titles, labelled axes with units, a consistent scale and no unnecessary decoration. A one-page summary with the key indicators and short comments is often more useful to a manager than many pages of tables.

Interpreting results

  1. Identify what is above or below target or benchmark.
  2. Look for causes in the supporting records: rainfall, disease outbreaks, input changes, labour problems.
  3. Separate controllable causes from uncontrollable ones.
  4. Recommend actions and indicate how results will be monitored.

Example: block 7 yields 4.1 t/ha against a farm average of 5.6 t/ha. Records show late planting and a skipped top-dressing. The recommendation focuses on planting dates and the fertiliser programme, not on cultivar.

Using software

Spreadsheets allow sorting, filtering, pivot tables and charts. Farm management software and herd systems calculate many indicators automatically, but managers must still understand the calculations to check that results make sense.

Key points

  • Performance indicators turn records into information for decisions.
  • Use mean, median and range to summarise and describe variation.
  • Compare over time, between units, against targets and benchmarks, like with like.
  • Choose tables, line graphs, bar charts or scatter plots to fit the message.
  • Interpret by finding causes and recommending monitored actions.
